fiches.title: Distributed Ledger Technology and Blockchains
fiches.subtitle: Hashes, keys, consensus and network types

blocks.text: A **distributed ledger** is a database replicated across many participants (nodes) with no central administrator. A **blockchain** is a type of distributed ledger in which transactions are grouped into **blocks**, each containing the cryptographic **hash** of the previous block — making past records practically immutable.

items: **Cryptographic hash**: a fixed-length fingerprint of data; any change in the data changes the hash.
**Public/private keys**: the private key signs transactions and proves ownership; whoever holds it controls the assets.
**Double-spending problem**: preventing the same digital unit from being spent twice without a trusted intermediary — solved by consensus.
**Smart contracts**: self-executing code stored on a blockchain (e.g., Ethereum); **oracles** feed them external data.

head: Proof of work (PoW)
Proof of stake (PoS)
rows: Cost of computing power; a 51% attack requires majority of hash power
Value at stake; misbehavior is punished by **slashing**

items: **Permissionless** (public): anyone can join and validate (Bitcoin, Ethereum).
**Permissioned** (private/consortium): only approved participants validate — faster, more control, less decentralization.
**Layer 1** (base blockchain) vs. **layer 2** (scaling solutions built on top, e.g., rollups, Lightning).
**Forks**: protocol changes — a hard fork is not backward compatible and can split the chain.

blocks.text: **Consensus** replaces the trusted third party. Proof of work = security through computing power (energy-hungry); proof of stake = security through staked tokens, with **slashing** for misbehavior.

fiches.title: Cryptocurrencies, Tokens and DeFi
fiches.subtitle: Bitcoin, ether, stablecoins, DeFi and custody

items: **Bitcoin**: first cryptocurrency (2009); PoW; supply capped at 21 million coins, with issuance halving roughly every four years → positioned as “digital gold” / store of value.
**Ether**: native asset of Ethereum, a programmable smart-contract platform; used to pay transaction fees (gas).
**Native tokens (coins)** run on their own blockchain; **non-native tokens** are issued on an existing blockchain via smart contracts (e.g., ERC-20 tokens).
**Fungible** tokens are interchangeable; **non-fungible tokens (NFTs)** represent unique items.
**Utility** tokens give access to a service; **security** tokens represent financial claims (and fall under securities law).
**Tokenization** of real-world assets (funds, bonds, real estate) on blockchains.

head: Type
Backing
Main risk
rows: Cash and short-term securities held by the issuer
Reserve quality and transparency, issuer risk
Over-collateralized crypto locked in smart contracts
Supply adjusted by algorithms, little or no collateral
Loss of peg / death spiral (e.g., TerraUSD in 2022)

items: Financial services run by smart contracts without intermediaries: decentralized exchanges using **automated market makers** (liquidity pools), lending protocols, derivatives.
Risks: smart-contract bugs and hacks, oracle manipulation, governance attacks, regulatory uncertainty, impermanent loss for liquidity providers.

blocks.text: Losing a private key means losing the assets. **Cold storage** (offline) is safer than **hot wallets** (online). Holding assets on an exchange creates counterparty risk (e.g., the FTX collapse in 2022); institutions use qualified custodians and segregated accounts.
A **fiat-backed** stablecoin depends on the quality of its reserves; an **algorithmic** one risks a death spiral (TerraUSD). Native = its own blockchain; non-native = issued on another blockchain.

fiches.title: Allocating to Cryptocurrencies
fiches.subtitle: Risk, valuation approaches and position sizing

items: Very high volatility (historically about 40–80% a year for bitcoin, more for smaller tokens) and repeated drawdowns above 70%.
Fat tails and regime changes; correlation with equities (especially technology stocks) has **risen** since about 2020 and tends to increase in sell-offs.
Returns are driven by adoption, liquidity conditions, regulation and sentiment rather than cash flows.
**Equation of exchange**: $MV = PQ$ — value derived from the size of the economy the token serves and its velocity.
**Network value / Metcalfe’s law**: network value proportional to the square of the number of users.
**NVT ratio**: network value divided by on-chain transaction volume (a P/E-like metric).
**Cost of production** (PoW): mining cost as a floor-like reference.
**Store-of-value** comparison: share of the gold market capitalization.
Because volatility is so high, even small weights (1–5%) contribute a large share of portfolio risk → size positions by **risk contribution**, not by capital.
**Rebalancing** a small allocation systematically sells after rallies and buys after crashes.
Access: direct holdings with custodians, **spot ETFs/ETPs** (US spot bitcoin ETFs launched in January 2024), futures, trusts, crypto-related equities.
Risks beyond price: custody, exchange/counterparty, regulatory and tax, operational and fraud, liquidity in stress.

blocks.text: A 2% allocation is not 2% of the risk. With 70% volatility against 10% for the rest of the portfolio and a 0.3 correlation, a 2% bitcoin weight contributes about 6% of total portfolio volatility — and a 5% weight about 18%.
Size a crypto sleeve by its **risk contribution**: a small but very volatile weight carries a large share of total portfolio volatility.

formulas.name: Equation of exchange
formulas.vars: $M$ money supply (network value), $V$ velocity, $PQ$ value of economic activity.

cards.back: A database replicated and synchronized across many participants without a central administrator.
A fixed-length output that uniquely fingerprints data; any change to the input produces a different hash.
The risk that a digital token is spent more than once; blockchains solve it through consensus rather than a trusted intermediary.
A consensus mechanism in which miners compete to solve computational puzzles to add blocks; secure but energy-intensive.
A consensus mechanism in which validators lock up tokens as collateral to propose and validate blocks; misbehavior is penalized by slashing.
An attack in which an entity controlling the majority of mining power or stake can rewrite recent transactions or double-spend.
Permissionless: anyone can participate and validate. Permissioned: only approved entities can validate transactions.
Self-executing code on a blockchain that automatically enforces the terms of an agreement.
A service that supplies external, off-chain data (e.g., prices) to smart contracts.
A native token (coin) is the base asset of its own blockchain; a non-native token is issued on an existing blockchain through a smart contract.
A unique, non-interchangeable token representing ownership of a specific digital or physical item.
A token designed to maintain a stable value relative to a reference asset (usually the US dollar), via fiat reserves, crypto collateral or algorithms.
Decentralized finance: financial services such as trading and lending provided by smart contracts without traditional intermediaries.
A DEX mechanism that prices trades using a formula and liquidity pools rather than an order book.
Keeping private keys offline to protect crypto assets from online hacking.
The roughly four-yearly 50% cut in the block reward paid to miners, slowing new supply toward the 21 million cap.
Network value divided by on-chain transaction volume; a valuation metric compared to a price-to-earnings ratio.

questions.q: What makes past transactions on a blockchain practically immutable?
options: Each block contains the hash of the previous block, so altering one block changes all later hashes
A central administrator approves every change
Transactions are stored on a single secure server
Blocks are encrypted with the user’s password
questions.explain: Each block contains the **hash of the previous one**: changing an old block would break every later link and be rejected by consensus.

questions.q: Which consensus mechanism secures the network through validators who lock up tokens as collateral?
options: Proof of authority by a central bank
questions.explain: **Proof of stake**: validators lock up tokens, part of which is destroyed (**slashing**) if they cheat.

questions.q: Compared with proof of work, proof of stake mainly:
questions.explain: Proof of stake does not rely on computing power, so it uses far less **energy**. It does not remove every attack risk.

questions.q: The main problem that blockchain consensus solves without a trusted intermediary is:
questions.explain: Consensus ensures the same token is not spent **twice**, without a bank or clearing house.

questions.q: A blockchain on which only pre-approved institutions can validate transactions is:
questions.explain: Validation restricted to approved participants = a **permissioned** blockchain (private or consortium).

questions.q: An ERC-20 token issued through a smart contract on Ethereum is best described as:
options: A native coin of its own blockchain
questions.explain: Issued on an existing blockchain through a smart contract = a **non-native** token. Ether is Ethereum’s native token.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes an NFT from a cryptocurrency such as bitcoin?
options: Each NFT is unique and not interchangeable
NFTs are always backed by fiat currency
questions.explain: An **NFT** is unique (non-fungible); one bitcoin is interchangeable with another (fungible).

options: Unlimited but decided by miners each year
questions.explain: Bitcoin supply is capped at **21 million**; new issuance halves roughly every four years.

questions.q: Which type of stablecoin is most exposed to a “death spiral” in which loss of confidence breaks the peg?
options: Algorithmic stablecoins with little or no collateral
Fiat-backed stablecoins fully reserved in T-bills
questions.explain: With no collateral, an **algorithmic** stablecoin depends on confidence: TerraUSD collapsed in 2022.

questions.q: For a fiat-collateralized stablecoin, the primary risk to holders is:
options: The quality, liquidity and transparency of the issuer’s reserves
Smart-contract liquidation cascades of crypto collateral
questions.explain: Stability depends on the issuer’s **reserves**: their quality, liquidity and transparency (audits).

questions.q: Which is a risk specific to decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols?
options: Bugs or exploits in smart-contract code
Central bank intervention in the order book
questions.explain: In DeFi, code is the intermediary: a **bug or exploit** in a smart contract can drain a protocol.

questions.q: Storing private keys offline to protect crypto assets from hacking is called:
questions.explain: **Cold storage** keeps private keys offline. A hot wallet is connected to the internet and more exposed.

questions.q: The collapse of a large crypto exchange in 2022 mainly highlighted which risk for investors who left assets on the platform?
questions.explain: Leaving assets on a platform creates **counterparty risk**: if it fails or misuses funds, clients lose their holdings.

questions.q: Why should an allocation to bitcoin be sized by risk contribution rather than by capital weight?
options: Its very high volatility means a small weight can account for a large share of portfolio risk
Its volatility is lower than that of bonds
Its correlation with equities is always −1
questions.explain: With volatility five to eight times higher, a small weight produces a **large share of total risk**.

questions.q: Since around 2020, the correlation of bitcoin with equities (especially technology stocks) has generally:
options: Become irrelevant because bitcoin stopped trading
questions.explain: Correlation with (tech) equities has **risen** since institutional investors arrived, especially in sell-offs, which weakens the diversification benefit.

questions.q: Which valuation approach for cryptocurrencies relies on the equation of exchange $MV = PQ$?
options: Estimating token value from the economic activity it supports and its velocity
Comparing book value to market value
questions.explain: The **equation of exchange** links network value (M) to the economic activity served (PQ) and to velocity (V).

questions.q: Metcalfe’s law, used to value networks, states that a network’s value is proportional to:
options: The square of the number of users
The square root of the token supply
questions.explain: **Metcalfe’s law**: value ∝ n² (the number of possible connections between users).

questions.q: A portfolio with 10% volatility adds a 3% allocation to bitcoin (volatility 70%, correlation 0.3) by reducing the rest proportionally. The new portfolio volatility is closest to:
questions.explain: $\sigma^2 = 0.97^2 \times 0.01 + 0.03^2 \times 0.49 + 2 \times 0.97 \times 0.03 \times 0.3 \times 0.1 \times 0.7 = 0.009409 + 0.000441 + 0.001222 = 0.011072$, so $\sigma \approx 10.5\%$. Just 3% of capital in bitcoin adds about half a point of volatility.
